As a platform owner, my console identity cannot act inside a tenant except through audited impersonation so that tenant data stays protected.
As the platform, I enforce minimum strength and hash with argon2id so that credentials resist offline cracking.
As the platform, I rate limit login attempts and lock accounts after repeated failures so that credential stuffing fails.
As a user and as an admin, I can see recent logins with device and location so that suspicious access is visible.
As a tenant admin, I can suspend a user so that all their sessions and tokens are invalidated immediately.
As a tenant admin, I can issue, rotate, and revoke API keys for BYO integrations so that external systems authenticate without user credentials.
As the platform, I log every login, failed login, password change, role change, and key rotation to the audit log so that security events are traceable.
As a tenant admin on an enterprise plan, I can restrict staff logins to approved IP ranges so that office-only access is enforced.
As a tenant admin on enterprise plan, I can configure SAML/OIDC SSO so that my staff uses corporate identity providers.
As a tenant admin, I sync users from my identity provider via SCIM so that staff onboarding is automated.
As a trader, I can log in with magic link or WebAuthn so that I avoid password fatigue.
As a tenant admin with permission, I force logout all sessions of a specific trader without a full suspension, so that I can respond to suspected compromise proportionally.

As support staff with permission, I reset a trader or staff 2FA enrollment after identity checks, with audit and a cooldown on sensitive actions, so that a lost device does not permanently lock an account.

As the platform, I require a fresh 2FA challenge for sensitive actions such as payout method change, role change, and bulk suspension, so that a stolen session cannot perform high-risk operations.
As the platform, I record which version of terms, privacy, and risk disclaimer each user accepted at registration and re-accept after changes, so that legal consent is provable per trader.
As the platform, I block disposable email domains, rate limit registrations per IP, and require a bot challenge on signup, so that fake account farms become expensive to run.
As the platform, login, password reset, and invite flows return identical responses for known and unknown emails, so that attackers cannot harvest valid accounts.
As a tenant admin, I configure session lifetimes and remember-me policy separately for traders and staff, so that session risk matches firm policy.
As a trader, I close my own account only when no open positions, pending payouts, or open risk cases exist, with a retention notice, so that closure is safe and compliant.
As staff, I merge duplicate trader identities belonging to one person across multiple emails with audit and consolidated history, so that abuse analysis and CRM see one person.
As a user, I view and revoke devices trusted for 2FA step-up exemption, so that a lost device can be untrusted remotely.
As the platform, I enforce staff password expiry and block reused passwords, so that staff credentials meet enterprise tenant expectations.
As a super admin, I can create, view, edit, suspend, and terminate a tenant so that each prop firm has an isolated workspace.
As the platform, I resolve the tenant from the request domain or subdomain at the edge so that branding, config, and data scope are correct for every request.

As a tenant admin, I can view delivery attempts, response codes, and payloads so that I can debug my own integration without asking support.
As a tenant admin, I can send a test event to my endpoint so that I can validate my integration before going live.

As the notifications module, I consume lifecycle events so that emails and in-app alerts fire without any producer calling me directly.
As the reports module, I consume events to maintain read models so that analytics never query operational tables.
As the platform, every event carries tenant_id and every consumer enforces tenant scope so that cross-tenant leakage through events is impossible.

master_backlog.story: As ops, I can view dead letter events with error context, filter by consumer group and error type, and selectively retry or discard them, so that poison events are diagnosed and recovered without production hacks.

As ops, given a triggering event ID, I can trace every downstream consumer that processed it, their processing duration, and success or failure, so that multi-hop event flows are debuggable end to end.
As ops, I track per-consumer-group latency from event emission to successful processing, with configurable SLA thresholds and alerts on breach, so that slow consumers are caught before they cascade.

As the platform, I route critical events (breach, enforcement, payout approval) through a high-priority stream that cannot be starved by analytical or notification events, so that money-impacting processing is never delayed by volume spikes.

As the platform, I track per-endpoint success rate, average latency, and consecutive failures, auto-disable endpoints after sustained failure, and alert the tenant admin, so that broken integrations surface without manual checks.
As the platform, CI runs automated compatibility tests on every event schema change verifying no existing consumer breaks, so that schema evolution never silently breaks downstream modules.

As a client, I can send an idempotency key on mutating requests so that a retry after a timeout never double-creates an order, payout, or account.
As the platform, I enforce maximum body size and per-route timeouts so that oversized or slow requests cannot exhaust workers.
As ops and the orchestrator, I can probe liveness and readiness so that deploys and restarts are safe and traffic shifts only to healthy instances.
As a developer or tenant integrator, I get an auto-generated OpenAPI spec per route group so that integration work is self-serve.
As a tenant machine client, I authenticate with a tenant API key scoped to permitted routes so that integrations never use user sessions.
As the platform, I mark sensitive routes such as payout approval, rule changes, and role changes for mandatory audit logging so that critical actions are always recorded.
As a client, I receive a consistent error envelope with code, message, and correlation id so that all three frontends handle failures uniformly.
As a tenant developer, I can call a sandbox tenant with test data so that I can integrate without touching production.
As the platform, I rely on Cloudflare for WAF, DDoS, and bot mitigation and restrict origin access so that edge and app layers do not duplicate controls.

As a client, every list endpoint returns cursor-based pagination with a next cursor and consistent shape, so that trader, account, payout, and ticket lists paginate uniformly and no list grows unbounded.
As the platform, I check the tenant's module entitlements before routing so that routes for disabled modules return a clean 404 and tenants only reach capabilities they purchased.

As a client, I submit batch mutations with a defined maximum size and receive partial-failure responses with per-item status, so that bulk operations like payout approval and account actions are atomic per item and auditable.
As the platform, I provide a standardized multipart and streaming upload contract with size and type limits for KYC documents and support attachments, so that file endpoints are consistent and safe.
As ops, I define explicit PII fields per route and enforce scrubbing rules in request logs, so that GW-10 structured logging never leaks emails, identity data, or payment data.

As the platform, I emit Sunset and Deprecation headers on versioned routes and publish a sunset schedule, so that integrators are warned before breaking changes and the SDK-15 changelog stays accurate.
As the platform, I include Retry-After headers on 429 responses and document backoff behavior, so that clients and webhooks retry predictably instead of hammering the API.
As a client, every successful response uses a consistent data envelope matching the error contract in GW-18, so that frontends and integrators parse responses uniformly.
As the platform, I define idempotency key expiry, tenant scope, and storage, so that GW-12 idempotency keys do not grow unbounded and cannot collide across tenants.
As the platform, I return a branded maintenance response when CON-16 maintenance mode is active, with read-only pass-through where configured, so that planned downtime is enforced at the gateway.
As the platform, every service including api, workers, relay, bot, and frontends runs as a Docker image built in CI so that all environments are identical.

v1_execution.story: As a trader, I can create an account with email and password on my prop firm's domain so that I belong to that firm's tenant.
As any user, I can log in with email and password and be placed in the correct tenant context from the domain so that I only see my firm's data.
As a user, I can reset a forgotten password through a single-use email link so that I regain access securely.
As the platform, I issue short-lived JWT access tokens with rotating refresh tokens and server-side revocation so that stolen tokens expire quickly.
As a tenant admin or staff member, I must enroll TOTP two-factor at first login so that financial operations are protected.
As the platform, I define Super Admin, Tenant Admin, custom staff roles, Trader, and API Consumer so that access maps to responsibility.
As the platform, I enforce permission keys declared by each module in resource.action format at the API layer so that modules plug in without custom auth code.
As the platform, I restrict every query and action to the caller's tenant inside the data layer so that cross-tenant access is impossible by construction.
As a platform owner, my console identity cannot act inside a tenant except through audited impersonation so that tenant data stays protected.
As the platform, I enforce minimum strength and hash with argon2id so that credentials resist offline cracking.
As a tenant admin, I can suspend a user so that all their sessions and tokens are invalidated immediately.
As a super admin, I can create, view, edit, suspend, and terminate a tenant so that each prop firm has an isolated workspace.
As the platform, I resolve the tenant from the request domain or subdomain at the edge so that branding, config, and data scope are correct for every request.
As the platform, I inject the caller's tenant id into every repository query so that no module can read another tenant's rows.
As a super admin, I can enable or disable modules per tenant so that each firm gets exactly the capabilities it purchased.
As a tenant admin, I can store my broker credentials, payment provider keys, KYC settings, and email sender config so that integrations run under my own accounts.
As the platform, I encrypt tenant integration secrets at rest and never return them in logs or API responses so that credentials stay safe.
As a super admin, I can suspend a tenant so that logins, new orders, and payouts stop immediately while all data is preserved.
As the platform, I prefix every tenant file in object storage by tenant id so that documents and certificates never mix between firms.
As a module developer, I write domain state and an outbox row in one database transaction so that no event is lost and no event is emitted for a rolled-back transaction.
As the platform, a dedicated relay process polls the outbox and publishes events to Redis Streams so that delivery survives application restarts.
As the platform, every event carries id, type, version, tenant_id, occurred_at, and payload so that consumers can evolve safely and scope correctly.
As a consumer module, I deduplicate by event id so that redelivery never causes double emails, double payouts, or double ledger entries.
As the platform, I persist every published event to an append-only log table so that replay and audit are always possible.
As a module owner, I use shared utilities to verify provider signatures and deduplicate by provider event id so that payment and KYC webhooks are handled consistently and idempotently.
As the platform, I keep broker commands in a separate Postgres command table with retry and backoff so that commands, which are requests, are never confused with events, which are facts.
As the platform, I expose one API with trader, admin, console, and webhook route groups so that surface separation is enforced at the routing layer.
As the platform, I resolve the tenant from the request domain or subdomain and reject unknown hosts so that no request ever executes without tenant context.
As the platform, I verify JWTs or API keys on every protected route and reject invalid credentials so that anonymous access is impossible.
As the platform, I enforce module-declared permission keys per route so that a user only reaches routes their role allows.
As the platform, I apply per-IP and per-user rate limits with clear 429 responses so that abuse and runaway clients cannot degrade the platform.
As a client, I can send an idempotency key on mutating requests so that a retry after a timeout never double-creates an order, payout, or account.
As a client, I receive a consistent error envelope with code, message, and correlation id so that all three frontends handle failures uniformly.
As the platform, every service including api, workers, relay, bot, and frontends runs as a Docker image built in CI so that all environments are identical.
As DevOps, I run production as a defined Compose stack on Hetzner so that deployment is reproducible without Kubernetes overhead.
As a developer, every push runs lint, typecheck, unit tests, and image build so that broken code never reaches main.
As DevOps, merging to main deploys to staging automatically and production deploys only via manual approval so that releases are controlled.
As the platform, I run versioned migrations with expand-contract discipline so that schema changes never cause downtime.

As the platform, I run PgBouncer in front of Postgres with per-service pool sizing so that the API and workers never exhaust connections during sync bursts or deploy spikes.

As the platform, on payment captured I post customer payment credit and settlement receivable so that revenue enters the ledger at the source.

v1_execution.feature: Container image registry and immutable tagging
v1_execution.story: As DevOps, every CI build pushes a container image to a defined registry with an immutable tag (commit sha) alongside a moving tag (env), and production deploys reference the immutable tag, so that what is deployed is reproducible and rollback targets a specific image.

v1_execution.feature: Container resource limits and host capacity plan
v1_execution.story: As DevOps, every service runs with explicit CPU and memory limits in the Compose stack, and the host is sized with documented headroom for peak sync and enforcement bursts, so that one runaway container cannot exhaust the host and take down the API.

v1_execution.feature: Backup integrity verification and automated restore drill
v1_execution.story: As DevOps, a scheduled job verifies last night’s Postgres backup restores to a scratch environment within RTO, and alerts on failure, so that a silent corrupt backup never survives until a real incident.

v1_execution.feature: Audit log access and export audit
v1_execution.story: As the platform, every view, search, and export of audit logs is itself recorded with actor, filters, and result count, so that access to audit data is accountable.
As the platform, staff access to KYC documents, payout methods, and personal data is audited with actor, reason, permission, and entity, so that sensitive data access is provable.
As platform staff, I see a consistent console shell with navigation, layout, and routing for all platform console features so that I can access every console capability without ad-hoc pages.

As platform staff, my console session expires after inactivity, requires re-authentication for sensitive actions, and can be revoked by another super admin, so that a stolen console session cannot be used indefinitely.
As the platform, every adapter passes a shared contract test that proves the capability interface is honoured, so that swapping adapters is a verified operation, not a promise.
As the platform, broker credentials are encrypted with a documented scheme and rotated on a defined schedule, so that a credential leak is bounded and recoverable.

v1_execution.feature: Rule set migration for existing accounts
v1_execution.story: As a tenant admin, when I edit a rule set I see how in-flight accounts are affected and choose the migration policy, so that rule edits never retroactively alter accounts by accident.
As the platform, a golden-case regression suite proves that evaluation decisions do not drift across releases, so that rule changes are safe.
As support, I can force re-evaluation of a single account after a corrected snapshot, so that edge cases do not become engineering tickets.
As the platform, I validate chain-specific crypto address format before submission, so that payouts to invalid addresses are blocked before money leaves.
As a trader, I can download a proper invoice for each purchase, so that I have it for accounting.
As the platform, client retries on checkout submit never double-create an order, so that duplicate charges cannot occur.

v1_execution.feature: KYC document upload progress and retry

As the platform, a scheduled worker expires abandoned checkout sessions after the reservation window, marks them expired, releases the reserved coupon and price holds, and emits a checkout.session.expired event through the outbox so that stale reservations never corrupt a later order.

v1_execution.story: As the platform, I evaluate fail conditions before pass conditions, and review conditions before warnings, so that a trader cannot "pass" on the same trade that breaches a risk rule.

v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Extracted from PDF Module 10 decision engine specification.

v1_execution.story: As the platform, I deduplicate enforcement jobs by instance and a short time window so that simultaneous breach events on the same account never create duplicate enforcement jobs.
v1_execution.notes: PDF Module 12 concurrency protection. Critical for flash-crash scenarios.

v1_execution.story: As the platform, I maintain a canonical metric registry that defines every rule metric (daily loss, drawdown, PnL, consistency, trading days) with its exact mathematical formula, basis (equity or balance), inclusion of floating PnL, commissions, swaps, and adjustments, and precision rules, so that two tenants who both configure "5% daily loss" evaluate identically under the same rule set.
v1_execution.notes: Foundational layer between canonical snapshot and rule evaluation. Prevents semantic drift across tenants. Without this, two challenges can both say "5% daily loss" and mean different things.
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

v1_execution.story: As the platform, I provide a canonical trading calendar and time context that defines trading day boundaries, day reset time, DST handling, holiday calendars, trading sessions, weekend windows, broker time versus platform time, and challenge start and expiry, so that every rule consumes a standard time context instead of embedding its own assumptions.
v1_execution.notes: Every rule should consume the same time context. Complements EVL-27 (daily reset timezone) and BRG-28 (broker server time drift).
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

v1_execution.story: As the platform, I maintain an internal representation of every rule and a dependency map from rule to metrics, so that when a metric changes only the rules that depend on it are re-evaluated, and composite rules such as phase pass can be expressed as expressions over primitive rules.
v1_execution.notes: V1 uses a fixed rule catalog but still needs the internal IR and dependency map. Tenant-authored DSL stays EVL-24 in V3.
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

v1_execution.story: As the platform, I store two distinct snapshot types: a BrokerSnapshot that records exactly what the broker reported, and an EvaluationSnapshot that links to a BrokerSnapshot, records derived metrics, and records the rule set version used, so that any breach decision can be answered with the precise state that was known when the decision was made.
v1_execution.notes: Critical for disputes and replay. Answers "what exactly did the system know when it failed this account" without relying on vendor state.
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

v1_execution.feature: Rule trigger matrix and observation requirements
v1_execution.story: As the platform, I classify every rule by the observation pattern it requires (fast risk stream, position or trade event, periodic sync, time or event, or behavioural batch), and I route each rule to the correct observation path, so that raw market ticks are never piped into the rule engine and no critical breach rule is left on a slow periodic poll.
v1_execution.notes: This classification determines which rules need streaming, which need event triggers, and which can run periodically. Ties directly to EVL-05, EVL-26, and BRG-21.
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

v1_execution.feature: Fast risk guard and emergency threshold path
v1_execution.story: As the platform, I run a deliberately small and independently testable fast risk guard that watches only catastrophic thresholds such as max daily loss and max drawdown on the highest-frequency observation path available, so that a bug in the full rule evaluator cannot leave a funded account unbounded.
v1_execution.notes: Independent backstop, not a second rule engine. Only catastrophic thresholds. Feeds the same Enforcement Coordinator as the primary path.
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

v1_execution.story: As the platform, I enforce strict ordering on trading snapshots so that a late-arriving snapshot never overwrites newer state, and I enter a defined DATA_STALE state when the observation path stops delivering updates near a threshold, so that stale or out-of-order broker data never drives a breach or a payout.
v1_execution.notes: Tightens LCC-28 (currently V2) for the V1 breach path. Without this, a delayed snapshot can trigger a false breach or mask a real one.
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

v1_execution.feature: Precision, rounding and threshold comparison semantics
v1_execution.story: As the platform, I define explicit precision, rounding, and comparison semantics for every metric, including account currency rounding, broker-reported versus platform-derived equity, strict or inclusive threshold comparison, and tolerance buffers, so that a trader and the platform never disagree on whether a threshold was crossed.
v1_execution.notes: Prevents the "trader sees $95,000.00, platform computed $94,999.996" class of dispute. Complements EVL-30 threshold tolerance buffers.
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

v1_execution.story: As the platform, I maintain a versioned test vector suite covering day-start equity vs balance, floating PnL, commissions, swaps, deposits and withdrawals, partial closes, broker corrections, DST day reset, trailing drawdown high-water mark, threshold tolerance, stale snapshots, and out-of-order snapshots, so that the rule semantics are executable and regressions are caught before release.
v1_execution.notes: Expands EVL-35 into the explicit edge-case suite from the rule-engine research. The test vectors become part of the rule specification.
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

v1_execution.story: As the platform, every breach decision carries an idempotency key composed of tenant id, account id, rule version, and breach epoch, so that the same breach detected repeatedly results in exactly one logical breach, one account state transition, and one enforcement workflow.
v1_execution.notes: Complements LCC-41 (double-enforcement prevention). Together they guarantee one-breach-one-enforcement even under sync replay or multi-worker races.
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

v1_execution.feature: Partial enforcement state and per-position confirmation
v1_execution.story: As the platform, when enforcement closes some but not all positions, the account enters ENFORCEMENT_PARTIAL and the system continues reconciliation until every position is confirmed closed or an escalation policy fires, so that a partial liquidation is never marked FAILED.
v1_execution.notes: Adds ENFORCEMENT_PENDING, ENFORCEMENT_PARTIAL, ENFORCED, and FAILED as distinct enforcement states. Complements LCC-39 (per-ticket closure log).
v1_execution.team_comments: 9/18/2026 Added from rule-engine research gap analysis.

tooling_register.why_rejected: Vanta and Drata are commercial (~$15k+/yr). In-house evidence pipeline is a full build. Comp AI is the open-source equivalent.
tooling_register.exit_path: Evidence is exported to standard formats. Policies are documents.
tooling_register.notes: Adopt in V2 when SOC 2 readiness becomes a sales requirement. Do not build evidence collection in-house.

tooling_register.replaces_building: Building compliance automation and Trust Center in-house
tooling_register.why_this_one: Developer-first platform for automated compliance, risk management, and Trust Center. Apache-2.0 licence is more permissive than Comp AI's AGPL.
tooling_register.why_rejected: Comp AI is AGPL. If licence matters, Openlane is the permissive alternative with similar capability.
tooling_register.exit_path: Compliance data exports to CSV / JSON.
tooling_register.notes: Evaluate alongside Comp AI in V2. Pick whichever fits the licence model better.

tooling_register.replaces_building: Building an e-signature flow for funded account agreements
tooling_register.why_this_one: Open-source e-signature platform. The DocuSign alternative. Self-hosted, legally binding, audit trail included. Eliminates per-envelope pricing.
tooling_register.why_rejected: DocuSign and HelloSign are per-envelope commercial. In-house build is out of scope. Documenso is the open-source equivalent.
tooling_register.exit_path: Signed PDFs and audit trails are portable standard formats.
tooling_register.notes: Adopt in V2 when DOC-12 (Contract e-signature) lands. Replaces the DocuSign/HelloSign choice already flagged in Tooling Register.

tooling_register.replaces_building: Building API key management, rate limiting, and usage analytics in-house
tooling_register.why_this_one: Purpose-built API key management. Handles issuance, rotation, revocation, per-key rate limits, usage analytics, and scoped access. Serves the tenant API key lifecycle without in-house cryptography and rate limiting.
tooling_register.alternatives_considered: In-house API keys, Zuplo, Kong key auth
tooling_register.why_rejected: In-house build is error-prone for cryptographic keys. Kong is overkill. UnKey is the focused tool for this single problem.
tooling_register.exit_path: Keys are standards-compliant; verification is stateless.
tooling_register.notes: Adopt in V2 when AUTH-21 (Tenant API keys) lands. Provides rate limiting and analytics for free.

tooling_register.replaces_building: Building a multi-tenant identity provider in-house
tooling_register.why_this_one: Multi-tenant identity provider built for SaaS. Customizable login experiences, comprehensive user management, role-based access control, and organisation support. Directly serves AUTH-13, AUTH-15, TEN-03.
tooling_register.why_rejected: Better Auth is more framework-agnostic and lighter. Logto is more opinionated with richer UI. Evaluate in V2 if Better Auth becomes limiting.
tooling_register.exit_path: Standard OAuth2 / OIDC. Users are portable.
tooling_register.notes: Alternative to Better Auth for V2/V3. Evaluate only if Better Auth hits a wall on multi-tenant organisations or SCIM.

tooling_register.why_this_one: Comprehensive self-hosted identity provider with SAML, OIDC, LDAP, and proxy auth. MIT licence. Serves AUTH-24 (SSO federation) and AUTH-25 (SCIM provisioning) when enterprise tenants need to bring corporate identity providers.
tooling_register.why_rejected: Keycloak is heavier. Zitadel is Apache-2.0 but less established. Okta and Entra are commercial. Authentik is the leading self-hosted choice.
tooling_register.exit_path: SAML and OIDC are standard protocols. Users are portable.
tooling_register.notes: Adopt in V3 when enterprise tenants require SSO. Do NOT introduce in V1/V2 — overkill until a paying tenant demands it.

tooling_register.replaces_building: Building tenant marketing email and newsletter infrastructure
tooling_register.why_this_one: Self-hosted email platform for newsletters, marketing automation, and drip sequences. Open-source Mailchimp alternative. Serves tenant marketing email when CRM module lands.
tooling_register.why_rejected: Listmonk is newsletter-only. Mailchimp and SendGrid Marketing are commercial. Plunk handles both transactional-adjacent and marketing in one self-hosted platform.
tooling_register.exit_path: Subscriber lists and templates are portable.
tooling_register.notes: Adopt in V3 with the CRM module. Not for transactional email — Postmark / Resend remain the choice for those.

tooling_register.replaces_building: Building pre-built API connectors for BYO Integration SDK
tooling_register.serves_req_ids: SDK-01, SDK-04, SDK-08, SDK-11, SDK-12, SDK-13
tooling_register.why_this_one: Integration platform with 500+ pre-built API connectors, unified data models, and OAuth handling. Serves the BYO Integration SDK (SDK module) by providing pre-built connector infrastructure instead of hand-coding each integration.
tooling_register.why_rejected: Composio is AI-agent focused. In-house connector library is a large build. Nango is the mature open-source integration platform.
tooling_register.notes: Elastic-2.0 licence — verify commercial use terms before adopting. Evaluate in V3 when BYO SDK module lands.
